title: Wings as eagles (Isaiah 40:31)
hook: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachamu: comfort, comfort, a job handed out to a group. Your line was comfort ye my people. Did your message reach someone's heart? Today, the end of the same chapter. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

Near the end of Isaiah forty, the prophet quotes the people's complaint back to them. Jacob is saying: my way is hidden from the Lord, my cause is passed over. Nobody sees what this is costing me. The prophet answers with a question, hast thou not known?, and says the Lord fainteth not. Then he grants that the tiredness is real for people, and goes further: even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. The strongest runners in town give out. So where does strength come from, if not from being young? The chapter's last verse answers, and it's a verse with wings in it.
screen: `MY WAY IS HIDDEN FROM THE LORD.` → `EVEN THE YOUNG FALL.` → `THE LAST VERSE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The verse reads: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Start with the condition. Not they that try harder. Not they that are young. They that wait. In this verse, strength isn't something you grind out; it's something given back while you wait. Some translations render that verb as they that hope. Now look at the order of the promise. Fly. Run. Walk. If you were writing a pep talk, you'd build up: walk, then run, then soar. Isaiah goes the other way. Some readers hear that as honest. There are days of wings. There are days you can run. And there are plenty of days when the most anyone can promise is that you'll walk and not faint. The verse counts that as strength too, and lists it last, where it has the final word. And the eagle itself: the Hebrew word is nesher, a great bird of the open sky. Some readers picture it rising on what's already moving in the air, not flapping its way up. Waiting, in this verse, looks less like doing nothing and more like that: being still enough to be carried. Jewish life builds that stillness into the week. Shabbat is one way a whole people practices stopping, so the strength can come back.
screen: `THEY THAT WAIT, OR THEY THAT HOPE.` · `FLY, RUN, WALK: THE ORDER GOES DOWN.` · `WALK, AND NOT FAINT, IS STRENGTH TOO.` · `AN EAGLE RISES ON MOVING AIR.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in order to renew. Until the bell, don't fix anything, plan anything or check anything. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Let today be whatever kind of day it is: a wings day, a running day, or a walking day. All three count. Just wait. If you pray, you can hold the verse's first words: they that wait upon the Lord. The bell holds the time.
Wings as eagles. From Isaiah forty, thirty-one: those who wait shall renew their strength, mount up, run, and walk and not faint. Today's word.
Your line: renew your strength. Today, take one real pause before you're empty, not after. And if it's a walking day, walking and not fainting counts. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read Isaiah 40 as part of the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and Shabbat is the weekly practice of stopping work so that body and spirit can rest.

fork.setup: you're worn out, and even the young and strong around you are falling. what does the verse say renews strength?
fork.reveal: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength." waiting, not effort, is the condition.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise that you'll soar.
what it means: those who wait get strength back, to fly some days, run some days, and walk without fainting on the rest.
what a scholar hears: the order goes down, fly, run, walk, and some translations render wait as hope.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): cut the narrator's own judgment 'maybe the deepest version' and replaced it with a plain observation about the verse's order.

Editor: hook no longer says the prophet doesn't argue (40:28 answers 'hast thou not known?'); dropped the etymology that the verb 'carries hope' (now: some translations render it 'hope'); eagle-soaring image softened to 'some readers picture'; removed 'two minutes'; varied the teach opener.

'Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall' is spoken (40:30 KJV) without quotation marks in the voice; it is listed under the paraphrase source. Confirm or add as a quote.
The Hebrew for 'wait' (qavah) also carries the sense of hope; stated as 'carries hope in it'. Confirm.
Nesher: some translators and lexicons suggest griffon vulture rather than eagle; the script says only 'a great bird of the open sky'. The soaring-on-air image is interpretive.
The fly-run-walk descending order as 'honest' is offered as 'some readers'.
